nameStory: The name 'water-milfoil' comes from the plant's feathery underwater leaves that look remarkably like the delicate, divided leaves of yarrow, which was once called 'milfoil' (meaning 'thousand leaves'). The 'Eurasian' part tells us this aquatic plant is originally from Europe and Asia, though it has traveled far from its native home. Just like yarrow's finely cut foliage, this water plant's leaves are so finely divided they create a soft, almost fur-like texture underwater.
description: Eurasian water-milfoil is a submerged aquatic plant that lives completely underwater except when it flowers. It grows in long, trailing stems that can reach several feet in length, creating dense underwater forests in lakes, ponds, and slow-moving streams. The plant is most recognizable by its distinctive feathery leaves that are arranged in whorls (circles) around the stem, giving it an almost Christmas tree-like appearance when viewed from the side. This non-native species has become very common in New England waters, sometimes growing so thickly it can clog waterways.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Feathery, bright green leaves arranged in whorls of 3-5 around the stem, divided into thread-like segments that feel soft and silky when you run them through your fingers underwater

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Long, trailing stems that grow completely submerged, often forming dense mats just below the water surface that can tangle around your legs or paddle

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny reddish or pink flowers emerge above water on spike-like stems in summer, looking like miniature bottlebrushes poking up from the surface

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Smooth, reddish-brown to green stems that feel firm but flexible, breaking with a clean snap when pulled apart

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: The entire plant feels soft and feathery to touch, almost like underwater fur, and doesn't have the coarse or slimy texture of many other aquatic plants

habitat: Found in lakes, ponds, slow-moving rivers, and even roadside ditches with standing water throughout New England. It prefers nutrient-rich waters and can grow in depths from just a few inches to over 20 feet deep. You'll often find it in the same waters as other aquatic plants like pondweeds and native water-milfoils, but it tends to dominate and crowd them out.

seasonality.spring: New growth begins as water warms, with fresh green shoots emerging from overwintering root crowns and stem fragments.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with dense underwater mats and distinctive red flower spikes poking above the water surface from June through August.
seasonality.fall: Plants begin to die back but stems may persist underwater, becoming brownish and more brittle to the touch.
seasonality.winter: Most above-ground growth dies back, but root crowns and stem fragments survive under ice to regrow next spring.

funFact: This plant is such a successful invader that a single stem fragment as small as your pinky nail can drift to a new location and grow into an entire colony that can clog a whole cove within just one or two growing seasons!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with native water-milfoils, but Eurasian water-milfoil typically has more leaflets per leaf segment (usually 12 or more fine divisions) compared to natives which often have fewer, slightly thicker segments. Remember: if the underwater 'Christmas tree' looks extra feathery and dense, it's probably the invasive Eurasian species.
contextualKnowledge: This plant is considered a highly invasive species in New England and is often the target of lake management efforts. Many lakes have programs to control or remove it because it can grow so densely that it interferes with swimming, boating, and fishing while crowding out native aquatic plants.
compareHints: Eurasian water-milfoil has more finely divided leaves than most of its native relatives, with leaflets that are thread-like and numerous. Native species like whorled water-milfoil tend to have slightly coarser, less densely packed leaf segments. The invasive species also tends to form much denser colonies and grows more aggressively than the native milfoils you might find in the same waters.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's water-milfoils, broadleaf water-milfoil stands out for having distinctly broader surface leaves compared to most relatives like Eurasian water-milfoil.
Low water-milfoil is the shortest member of its genus in New England, staying under a foot tall while Eurasian water-milfoil can reach 10 feet long.
Unlike its native milfoil cousins that stay mostly submerged, parrot's feather boldly emerges above water with bright green foliage.
Among New England's water-milfoils, Slender Water-milfoil lives up to its name with the most delicate, thread-like leaf divisions.
Unlike the aggressive Eurasian water-milfoil which forms dense mats, alternate water-milfoil grows in looser colonies and has its distinctive alternately-arranged flowers rather than whorled ones.
Siberian water-milfoil differs from other milfoils by its relatively short flower spikes and less aggressive spreading habit compared to invasive species like Eurasian water-milfoil.
Unlike the invasive Eurasian water-milfoil which has leaves scattered along the stem, whorled water-milfoil has its distinctive whorled leaf arrangement.
